kurz: Why the quotation currency of a fund plays no role in its currency risk, what hedging costs and why the decision turns out differently for equities and bonds.

bloecke.md:
## Three currency levels of a fund

A world ETF can be quoted in US dollars or in euros, or offer both through two share classes. This makes no difference to currency risk. The **quotation currency** only determines the unit of account in which the price of a fund unit is expressed. It is a conversion at the end of the calculation chain and not a risk in itself.

Two other levels are what matter. The first consists of the **trading currencies of the securities held**. On 31 August 2026, the MSCI World consisted of 1,280 stocks from 23 developed markets, and the country weights correspond approximately to the currency weights. The second consists of the **business currencies of the companies**. A group listed in Zurich in Swiss francs that generates two thirds of its revenue in dollars and euros depends economically mainly on these two currencies. Many large companies also hedge their own cash flows themselves. The currency risk of a world index is therefore lower than the country weights suggest. It is not zero, however, because the companies hedge their operating cash flow and not their share price.

The most common misconception is: “I'll buy the euro share class, then I have no dollar risk.” The euro class of an unhedged world ETF, however, carries exactly the same currency risk as the dollar class; only the display is different. Only share classes that are explicitly labelled “EUR hedged” are hedged. You can recognise them by the suffix in the fund name and by their own ISIN.

bloecke.md:
## Measuring the currency effect

MSCI calculates the same index in several currencies. The local equity returns are identical in each case. The difference between the dollar and the euro series therefore results solely from the movement of the EUR/USD exchange rate. This makes it possible to calculate the currency contribution precisely for each year:

`Currency effect = (1 + return in EUR) ÷ (1 + return in USD) − 1`

Over the 25 years from 2001 to 2025, the MSCI World returned 7.77% a year gross in dollars and 6.81% in euros. One euro grew to €5.19, one dollar to $6.49. The currency contribution was therefore minus 0.89% a year, or minus 20% cumulatively, because the euro appreciated on balance over the period. More important than this average is the dispersion around it. With a standard deviation of around 9.2 percentage points, the annual values range between minus 16.8 (2003) and plus 15.2 (2005).

bloecke.titel: Currency effect on the MSCI World, 2001-2025
bloecke.unter: Green marks years in which the dollar helped the euro investor; over the whole period red slightly predominates, but in individual years the swings are far larger than the average.

bloecke.titel: From the dollar index to the euro return in 2025
bloecke.unter: A year that the US media regarded as a strong year on the stock market was only average for euro investors because of the exchange rate, without any wrong decision behind it.

bloecke.md:
## The dampening effect of the dollar

It would seem natural to assume that currency risk adds to equity risk and that the euro investor is therefore worse off. The data show the opposite. The standard deviation of calendar-year returns in 2001-2025 was 17.8% for the euro investor and 18.5% for the dollar investor. The maximum interim loss was minus 53.6% in euros and minus 57.5% gross in dollars.

The reason is a negative correlation. In the seven years in which the index lost ground in dollars, the currency contributed plus 3.1 percentage points on average. In the 18 years with gains, it cost 1.9 points on average. The correlation between the currency effect and the index return was −0.34. Economically, this is because the dollar is regarded as a safe-haven currency. When investors pull capital out of risky assets, they seek dollar liquidity. Campbell, Serfaty-de Medeiros and Viceira demonstrated this relationship for 1975-2005. According to their results, the dollar, the euro and the Swiss franc move against world equity markets. For equity investors who want to minimise their risk, these currencies are therefore attractive, even though their average return is low.

bloecke.titel: The seven loss years 2001-2025 in dollars and euros

bloecke.md: The year 2002 was an exception. The index lost 19.5% in dollars but 31.7% in euros, because the currency effect of minus 15.15% worsened the loss by just over 12 percentage points. At the time, the euro was catching up after its weakness in 2000/01, and for once the flight to safety did not go into the dollar. The dampening effect of the dollar is therefore only a regularity and cannot be counted on as a reliable hedge.

## The cost of hedging

Hedging is done with currency forwards, each of which is replaced by a new one when it matures (rolling). Their price follows from an arbitrage condition and contains no forecast of the exchange rate. Under **covered interest parity**, a forward rate must reflect exactly the interest rate differential between the two currency areas. Otherwise, a risk-free profit could be made by borrowing in one currency and investing in the other.

It follows that when you hedge, you pay roughly the interest rate advantage of the foreign currency. If US interest rates are above European ones, an investor who hedges dollars pays the difference year after year, regardless of how the exchange rate develops. If the interest rate differential is the other way round, you receive money for hedging.

bloecke.formel: Forward rate (USD per EUR) = Spot rate × (1 + i_USD) / (1 + i_EUR)
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula describes covered interest parity. For the hedging costs from a euro perspective, the approximation is sufficient: cost per year ≈ i_USD − i_EUR. The sign can reverse; the formula applies in both directions.
variablen: current exchange rate in US dollars per euro
money market rate in the euro area for the term of the forward
money market rate in the US for the same term
bloecke.beispiel: Spot rate 1.1604 USD per euro (11 September 2026), euro money market 2.50% (ECB deposit facility rate since 16 September 2026), dollar money market 3.875% (midpoint of the Fed target range of 3.75-4.00% since 17 September 2026). One-year forward rate = 1.1604 × 1.03875 / 1.0250 = 1.1760. When selling dollars one year forward, you receive 0.8504 euros per dollar instead of 0.8618 on the spot market. That is 1.32% less and thus almost the interest rate differential of 1.375 percentage points.

bloecke.md: In 2019, the ECB deposit facility rate was minus 0.40% and, from 18 September, minus 0.50%, while the Fed target range was between 1.50% and 2.50%. Hedging dollar investments cost euro investors more than two percentage points a year at that time, more than the current yield of many European government bonds. Today it is around 1.4 points. Investors who hold a hedged fund for twenty years therefore do not know what the hedge will cost them. The only certainty is that they pay the prevailing interest rate advantage. In addition, there are the transaction costs of rolling monthly and a basis premium in the FX swap market. This premium rises in periods of stress, that is, precisely when the hedge is needed.

Hedged share classes hedge the net asset value as of a reference date, usually the end of the month. If the fund rises by 5% within the month, this increase is not hedged until the next roll. If the fund falls, it is over-hedged. In calm markets the deviation is negligible; in a crash month it is not. In addition, a “EUR hedged” class of a world fund hedges all index currencies against the euro. The costs are therefore a weighted average of many interest rate differentials and not just the US one.

## Currency risk in bonds

For bonds, the evidence is unusually clear, and the reason lies in the orders of magnitude. The Dimson-Marsh-Staunton database reports the average standard deviation of real returns for 20 foreign markets from 1900 to 2025. For equities it is 23.4% in local currency and 29.2% in dollars; for government bonds it is 14.9% and 20.6%. In both cases, the currency adds around six percentage points. For equities, that is a surcharge of a quarter on a risk that is already high. For bonds, it is a surcharge of almost 40%, and it applies to the risk of the very asset that is supposed to dampen fluctuations in the portfolio.

The balance of benefits and costs of hedging therefore turns out differently for bonds. For euro investors, an unhedged government bond in a foreign currency with a 3.5% yield and price fluctuations of a few per cent becomes a position whose result depends mainly on the exchange rate; the bond coupon merely comes on top. For an equity portfolio with an expected return of six to 7%, the 1.4 percentage points of hedging costs make up a fifth to just under a quarter of the return. In the defensive portion, they are the price of keeping that portion defensive at all.

bloecke.unter: Average standard deviation of real returns in 20 foreign markets from the perspective of a dollar investor; in absolute terms the surcharge is almost the same, in relative terms it is far larger for bonds.

bloecke.md:
## Implementation and taxation in Germany

Hedging takes place within the fund. Gains and losses from the currency forwards flow into the unit price and are only captured on sale or through the [[Advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)|advance lump sum (Vorabpauschale)]]. No separate taxable events arise as a result. For the [[Partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)|partial exemption (Teilfreistellung)]], the only thing that matters is the equity allocation to which the investment conditions commit the fund, under Section 2(6) InvStG (Investment Tax Act). An equity ETF that commits to more than 50% equity participations keeps the 30% partial exemption under Section 20(1) InvStG, whether it is hedged or not. Bond ETFs receive 0%, likewise regardless of currency hedging.

Investors who hedge themselves instead, for example with currency futures or currency certificates, generate capital income of their own. They have to pay tax on gains from the hedge, while the book loss in the portfolio remains unrealised. The Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) did at least abolish, without replacement, the former €20,000 limit on loss offsetting for derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte). For private investors, the fund solution nevertheless remains the simpler route in almost all cases.

- For the equity portion of a long-term global portfolio, the data speak against hedging. It certainly costs money and removes a dampening effect that historically occurred precisely in loss years.
- For the low-risk portion, the opposite applies. Bonds from outside the euro area should be held in the hedged version, because otherwise the defensive portion is not defensive.
- Make the decision once and record it in writing. After a bad year, it is tempting to buy the hedge that would have helped in hindsight. Doing so means speculating on the exchange rate instead of neutralising currency risk.

In institutional practice, there is a rule of thumb for investors who cannot decide. It is to hedge half of the foreign currency position. The rule is based on a consideration of regret in hindsight and not on optimisation. With full hedging, you are annoyed when the foreign currency rises; without hedging, when it falls. At 50%, the greatest possible regret in either direction is smallest, and only half the costs are incurred.

Mathematically, this is rarely optimal. As a remedy against the greater danger of changing the hedge ratio again after every price movement, the rule is nevertheless useful. For private investors in Germany, however, the approach usually fails in implementation. Half hedging requires two share classes of the same fund side by side, which have to be maintained twice and rebalanced against each other.

mitnehmen: The quotation currency of a fund says nothing about its currency risk; only the suffix “hedged” provides information about that.

Hedging costs correspond to the interest rate differential between the two currency areas and are not a fee; for dollars from a euro perspective, they are currently around 1.4 percentage points a year, and in 2019 they were over two.
For the MSCI World, the currency cost around 0.9 percentage points a year in 2001-2025 but reduced fluctuation and maximum loss, because the dollar rose in six of the seven loss years.
Whether hedging pays off depends on the ratio of currency fluctuation to the fluctuation of the investment itself, which is small for equities and large for bonds.
Sticking to a decision once it has been made is more important than the theoretically best hedge ratio.

begriffe.text: The currency in which a fund unit or an index is reported. It is purely a unit of account and says nothing about the currencies of the securities held and therefore nothing about currency risk.

Arbitrage condition under which the forward exchange rate exactly reflects the interest rate differential between two currency areas. It follows that hedging costs approximately equal the interest rate advantage of the foreign currency.
Contract that fixes an exchange rate today for a future date. Currency forwards are the building blocks of every currency hedge; funds usually roll them over monthly.

Share class of a fund whose foreign currency positions are hedged against a target currency, recognisable by the suffix “EUR hedged” and its own ISIN. The net asset value is hedged as of a reference date and not continuously.

The risk that changes in exchange rates alter the return measured in the home currency. It arises at the level of the securities' currencies and the companies' business currencies, not at the level of the fund's quotation.
